To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) ELLs are not monolingual, (b) the dominant academic discourse of policymakers in the United States has focused on improvement in English-language proficiency, (c) the mother tongue is a key component to literacy achievement for all ELL students, (d) there exist cultural and political tension in learning Standard English, (e) American Indian languages and culture are being lost as a result of education policies, and (f) language drift threatens the distinctiveness of ELLs.

(1) the dominant discourse in the U.S. for closing achievement gaps has focused solely on improvement and assessment for English language acquisition and (2) insufficient attention is being given to literacy achievement that does not come at the expense of mother tongue and the true cost of the measures implemented for English language literacy achievement for all ELL students.
the dominant discourse of policy makers and educators for closing literacy achievement for ELLs and AI/AN students is not inclusive of all students.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the dominant discourse of English literacy achievement is framed and how it is impacting American Indian/Alaskan Native and ELL students.
the following question: What is the impact of the current dominant academic discourse on the literacy achievement of English language learner (ESL) and American Indian/ Alaska Native (AIAN) students?

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the achievement gap is a complex problem that cannot be solved with a single solution.

the dominant academic discourse of the policy makers in the U.S. for closing literacy achievement for ELL and AINA students has focused on improvement of English-language acquisition and assessment of efficient learning of English, but insufficient attention has been paid to literacy achievement in the mother tongue.
the achievement of literacy in the mother tongue is a necessary and important part of the literacy development of ELLs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the dominant academic discourse of literacy achievement is a heteroglossic conversation that is in need of re-framing.

the achievement gaps between American Indian/Alaskan Native (AI/AN) students and English Language Learners (ELL) and their non-AI/AN and English-speaking peers can be narrowed through the use of culturally relevant pedagogy, which includes a focus on the mother tongue.
we are reframing the conversation on literacy achievement for ELLs and American Indian/ Alaska Native students by addressing the heteroglossia of the mother tongue and the dominant language.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the achievement gap for ELLs and American Indian/ Alaskan Native students cannot be closed without a deeper understanding of the complex linguistic, cultural, and political tensions that surround the teaching of English to these groups of students.
educators need to be aware of and address the heteroglossic tensions inherent in teaching Standard English to ELLs and American Indian/ Alaska Native (AIAN) students.
we need to reframe the dominant discourse of English literacy achievement to include the mother tongue and to acknowledge that language and literacy are not mutually exclusive.
